title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: At the little German spa where the Shtcherbatskys had settled — as in every place where people gather — the usual process of social crystallization went on, assigning every member a fixed and unalterable spot. Just as a particle of water in a frost locks itself into the precise form of a snow crystal, each new arrival at the springs was at once slotted into the place that fit them.
_Fürst_ Shtcherbatsky, _sammt Gemahlin und Tochter_, were immediately crystallized into a definite place — set there by the rooms they had taken, by their name, and by the company they fell in with.

That season a real German Fürstin happened to be visiting the spa, and the crystallizing process ran more briskly than ever. Princess Shtcherbatskaya wanted above all to present her daughter to this German princess, and the day after they arrived she duly carried out the ceremony. Kitty made a low, graceful curtsey in the _very simple_ — that is, very elegant — frock that had been ordered for her from Paris. The German princess said, "I hope the roses will soon come back to this pretty little face," and from that moment certain unbreakable lines were laid down for the Shtcherbatskys. They also got to know the family of an English Lady Somebody, a German countess and her son who had been wounded in the last war, a learned Swede, and M. Canut and his sister. But inevitably the Shtcherbatskys spent most of their time with a Moscow lady, Marya Yevgenyevna Rtishtcheva, and her daughter — whom Kitty disliked because she had fallen ill, like Kitty herself, over a love affair — along with a Moscow colonel Kitty had known since childhood, always seen until then in uniform and epaulettes, and now, with his little eyes, open neck, and flowered cravat, uncommonly ridiculous and tiresome, all the more because there was no shaking him off. Once the social pattern had set this firmly, Kitty grew badly bored, especially after the prince went away to Carlsbad and she was left alone with her mother. The people she already knew held no interest for her — nothing fresh would come of them. Her main entertainment at the spa became watching the people she did not know and inventing theories about them. It was characteristic of Kitty that she always pictured everyone in the best possible light, and never more so than with strangers. As she guessed at who people were, how they were connected, and what they were really like, she gave them the most extraordinary and noble characters, and then found confirmation of her guesses in everything she observed.

Of all these strangers, the one who attracted her most was a Russian girl who had come to the spa with an invalid Russian lady, Madame Stahl, as everyone called her. Madame Stahl belonged to the highest society, but she was so ill that she could not walk, and only on the rare fine day appeared at the springs in an invalid carriage. According to Princess Shtcherbatskaya, it was less her health than her pride that had kept Madame Stahl from making the acquaintance of any of the Russians there. The Russian girl looked after Madame Stahl, and Kitty noticed that she was also on easy terms with all the seriously ill people at the springs — and there were many of them — caring for them in the most unaffected way. The girl, as far as Kitty could gather, was not related to Madame Stahl, nor was she a paid attendant. Madame Stahl called her Varenka, and other people called her "Mademoiselle Varenka." Setting aside Kitty's curiosity about the girl's connection with Madame Stahl and with the other strangers, Kitty — as so often happened — felt herself drawn to Mademoiselle Varenka in a way she could not explain, and could tell when their eyes met that the feeling was mutual.

You could not quite say of Mademoiselle Varenka that she was past her first youth — she was more like a creature without youth at all; you might have taken her for nineteen or for thirty. Looked at feature by feature, she was handsome rather than plain, despite the sickly tinge of her face. Her figure would have been good too, if she had not been so painfully thin and her head so large for her medium height. Still, she was unlikely to attract men. She was like a fine flower already past its bloom and without fragrance, though its petals were not yet wilted. And she lacked precisely what Kitty had in such excess — the suppressed fire of vitality, the awareness of her own attractiveness.

She always seemed busy with work she could not possibly doubt the value of, and so seemed unable to be interested in anything outside it. That contrast with her own situation was exactly what made Mademoiselle Varenka so compelling to Kitty. Kitty felt that in her, in her whole way of life, she would find the example of what she was now so painfully searching for: an interest in life, a dignity in living — something quite apart from the social dealings between girls and men that now revolted her and looked to her like the shameless hawking of goods in search of a buyer. The more closely Kitty watched her unknown friend, the more convinced she became that this girl was the perfect creature she imagined, and the more eagerly she wanted to meet her.

The two girls passed each other several times a day, and each time Kitty's eyes were saying: "Who are you? What are you? Are you really the lovely creature I imagine? But please don't think," her eyes added, "that I would push myself on you — I simply admire you and like you." "I like you too, and you're very, very sweet. And I'd like you even more if I had the time," the eyes of the unknown girl answered. Kitty could see that she was always busy: taking the children of a Russian family home from the springs, fetching a shawl for a sick lady and tucking her into it, trying to amuse some peevish invalid, or choosing and buying cakes for someone's tea.

Soon after the Shtcherbatskys arrived, two new figures appeared in the morning crowd at the springs and drew universal — unfavorable — attention. There was a tall, stooping man with huge hands, dressed in an old coat too short for him, with black, plain, and yet alarming eyes; and a pockmarked, kind-faced woman, very badly and tastelessly dressed. Once Kitty recognized them as Russians, she had already begun, in her imagination, to spin a touching romance about them. But the princess, after consulting the visitors' register, found that this was Nikolay Levin with Marya Nikolaevna, and explained to Kitty what a bad man this Levin was — and all Kitty's fancies about the pair evaporated. It was less what her mother said than the fact that this was Konstantin's brother that made the two suddenly seem intensely unpleasant to Kitty. With his constant twitching of his head, Levin now provoked in her an uncontrollable feeling of disgust.
It seemed to her that his huge, terrible eyes, which kept following her, were full of hatred and contempt, and she tried to avoid crossing his path.
